For those how dont know 
The Coelacanth (pronounced SEE-luh-kanth) is a deep-sea predator that was widely believed by western science to have gone extinct roughly 66 million years ago along with the non-avian dinosaurs—until a living specimen was suddenly dragged up from the ocean floor in a fishing net off the coast of South Africa in 1938.
This unexpected capture stunned the scientific community. It shattered the prevailing understanding of vertebrate evolution. It firmly established the coelacanth as the ultimate "Lazarus taxon"—a biological group that completely vanishes from the fossil record only to miraculously reappear alive in the modern era.

The Shocking Rediscovery of 1938

Prior to December 1938, if you wanted to see a coelacanth, you had to look at a squashed fossil embedded in ancient shale. Paleontologists had carefully catalogued their unique bone structures, noted their abundance in the Devonian era, and confidently marked their extinction date at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Then came Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, a young museum curator in the small coastal city of East London, South Africa. Courtenay-Latimer maintained an agreement with local trawler captains: if they hauled up any unusual sea life, they would alert her before discarding it. On December 22, Captain Hendrik Goosen arrived in port with a bizarre, five-foot-long fish that his crew had pulled from a depth of roughly 240 feet near the mouth of the Chalumna River.
Courtenay-Latimer described the creature as a magnificent, iridescent blue fish with heavy, armored scales and limb-like fins. Sensing its immense scientific value, she carted the massive, rotting specimen back to her museum in a taxi. When local experts dismissed it as a mere shark or rock cod, she sketched the fish and sent a letter to J.L.B. Smith, an eccentric chemistry professor and passionate amateur ichthyologist at Rhodes University.
Upon seeing the sketch, Smith experienced a moment of utter disbelief. He famously wrote that his mind felt like it had exploded. He recognized the outline immediately as an animal that should not exist in the 20th century. By the time Smith arrived in East London, the fish had unfortunately been taxidermied and its soft internal organs thrown away. However, the skull and skeleton confirmed his wildest suspicion. He named the species Latimeria chalumnae in honor of the curator and the river where it was found. The discovery became a global media sensation, hailed as the biological equivalent of finding a living Tyrannosaurus rex wandering through a remote jungle.

Two Species and Two Oceans

For fourteen grueling years, Smith searched the western Indian Ocean for a second specimen to study its missing internal anatomy. He distributed thousands of leaflets along the African coast, offering a hefty cash reward for another "four-legged fish." In 1952, a second coelacanth was caught in the Comoro Islands, an archipelago situated between Mozambique and Madagascar. The Comorians, it turned out, were already quite familiar with the fish. They called it Gombessa, occasionally catching it by accident on deep-sea handlines and using its rough, sandpapery scales to scrub inner tubes or sand wood.
The Comoro Islands proved to be the primary home of the West Indian Ocean coelacanth. Decades later, a second distinct species was discovered entirely by accident halfway across the globe. In 1997, marine biologist Erdmann was on a honeymoon in Indonesia when his wife, Arnaz Mehta, spotted a strange, brownish-gold fish being wheeled through a fish market in Manado Tua, Sulawesi. Erdmann recognized it as a coelacanth, but noted it looked distinctly different from the African variety. Genetic testing later confirmed it as a separate species: Latimeria menadoensis, the Indonesian coelacanth.

A Highly Unusual Anatomy

The coelacanth is not just a standard fish that managed to hide well. Its physical anatomy is a bizarre mosaic of primitive features that separates it from almost every other living vertebrate on Earth.
• Lobed Fins: Most modern fish possess ray-fins, which are delicate webs of skin supported by thin bony spines. Coelacanths possess lobed fins. Their pectoral, pelvic, anal, and second dorsal fins are fleshy, muscular appendages attached to their bodies by a single, stout bone joint. These fins move in an alternating, diagonal rhythm. They mimic the exact walking gait of a four-legged land animal like a horse or a lizard.
• The Notochord: The coelacanth does not possess a solid, bony vertebral column. Instead, its back is supported by a thick, oil-filled tube of cartilage called a notochord. This primitive structure is an ancestral trait found in the earliest chordates. It is typically replaced by a true spine during embryonic development in almost all other modern vertebrates.
• The Intracranial Joint: The skull of the coelacanth is split completely in half by a unique, functional hinge joint. This intracranial joint allows the fish to tilt the entire front half of its head upward while feeding. This dramatically increases its gape and creates a powerful vacuum effect that sucks prey straight into its mouth. No other living vertebrate possesses a working joint inside its skull.
• The Rostral Organ: Located inside the snout of the coelacanth is a large, fluid-filled cavity with three distinct exterior openings. This is the rostral organ. It functions as a highly sensitive electroreceptor. It allows the fish to detect the faint, ambient electrical currents generated by the muscles of hidden prey in total darkness.
• A Tiny Brain in a Giant Skull: Despite having a massive, heavy skull that can weigh several pounds, the actual brain of an adult coelacanth is remarkably minuscule. It occupies a mere 1.5% of the total available cranial cavity. The remaining 98.5% of the skull is packed tight with a dense, heavy fat.

Behavior in the Deep Shadows

Because coelacanths reside at depths ranging from 300 to over 2,300 feet, observing them in their natural habitat requires specialized, deep-diving submersibles and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs). Over several decades of underwater observation, scientists have pieced together a clearer picture of their nocturnal lives.
During the harsh daylight hours, coelacanths are surprisingly social. They gather in small, peaceful groups inside underwater volcanic caves and deep basalt lava tubes. These caves shield them from powerful oceanic currents and larger predators like sharks. Inside these caverns, they remain almost motionless, hovering together without any signs of territorial aggression.
When darkness falls, they emerge from their caves individually to hunt along the steep submarine slopes. They are sluggish, low-energy swimmers, preferring to drift passively with the deep ocean currents rather than actively chase down meals. Their diet consists primarily of bottom-dwelling organisms, including lanternfish, cardinalfish, cuttlefish, and small crabs.
When hunting, they display a spectacular behavioral quirk known as a headstand. They will tilt their bodies entirely upside down, holding a vertical posture perpendicular to the sea floor for several minutes at a time. This headstand positions their specialized rostral organ just inches above the ocean floor, scanning the sand and rocky crevices for the electrical signatures of buried prey.

The Longest Lifespan in the Sea?

Recent scientific breakthroughs have revealed that the coelacanth operates on an incredibly slowed-down timeline. For many years, scientists calculated their age by counting growth rings on their scales, estimating their lifespan at around 20 years. However, a groundbreaking 2021 study utilizing advanced polarized light microscopy revealed that those rings were actually undercounted.
The updated data suggests that coelacanths live for up to 100 years, placing them among the longest-lived marine fish in the world alongside the Greenland shark. This slow pace of life extends directly to their reproduction. Coelacanths do not lay eggs. They are ovoviviparous, meaning the female retains the eggs inside her body until they hatch, eventually giving birth to fully formed, free-swimming young.
The internal gestation period for a female coelacanth is estimated to be an astonishing five years—longer than that of an elephant, and the longest documented gestation period of any animal on Earth. Furthermore, they reach sexual maturity exceptionally late in life, with males becoming fertile around age 40 and females around age 55.

Conservation and the Future

Today, both species of coelacanth are classified as threatened. The African coelacanth is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, while the Indonesian population is deemed Vulnerable. Because they reproduce so incredibly slowly and produce very few offspring at a time, their populations are highly vulnerable to sudden environmental disruptions.
Fortunately, they are not targeted by commercial fisheries. Their oily flesh is saturated with urea, wax esters, and foul-smelling compounds that make them completely unpalatable, causing severe digestive illness if consumed by humans. Instead, the greatest threat to their survival is accidental bycatch. Local artisanal fishermen targeting deep-water oilfish or sharks occasionally hook a coelacanth by mistake.
The coelacanth stands as a living reminder of how little we truly know about the deepest trenches of our oceans. Having survived multiple mass extinctions, continental drift, and the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs, this resilient survivor continues to drift quietly through the deep, black waters of the twilight zone.
